title: 8 Mac menu bar apps that actually earn their spot on a coding Mac (2026)
author: E Daugherty
summary: You know the moment. You glance up at the menu bar to check something and it's a wall of 25 icons, half of which you can't name. The MacBook notch has quietly eaten three of them. The menu bar is the most valuable real estate on a Mac, and most of us let it fill up by accident. Here's the short list of menu bar apps I'd actually let stay there on a Mac used for coding, and what each one earns its spot for. The rule I use An icon stays only if I look at it or click it at least once a day. Everything else gets hidden or quit. With that rule, these eight make the cut. 1. Ice (free, open source) Ice is the first thing I'd install, because it fixes the problem every other item on this list creates. It hides and shows menu bar items so you keep only the ones you care about visible. It's free, open source, and needs macOS 14 or later. If you've ever lost an icon behind the notch, this is the fix. 2. Stats (free, open source) Stats puts a system monitor in your menu bar: CPU, memory, disk, network, battery and more. You pick which modules show. Handy when a build, a Docker container or a local model suddenly makes the fans spin up and you want to know why. Install with brew install stats or grab the DMG from the releases page. 3. Itsycal (free) Itsycal is a tiny menu bar calendar that reads from the Mac Calendar app. You can see and create events, view and complete Reminders, and join virtual meetings from it. It has a configurable shortcut to open it, and yes, it supports Vim motions for navigation. 4. Maccy (free, open source) Maccy is a clipboard manager that does one job: keep your copy history and let you search it fast. Hit the shortcut, type, press Enter. It's keyboard-first, stores everything on your Mac, and is MIT licensed. It needs macOS 14 or later. Once you have clipboard history you stop re-copying the same error message three times. 5. Amphetamine (free on the Mac App Store) Amphetamine keeps your Mac awake with a simple switch in the menu bar, or automatically through Triggers. You can keep it awake indefinitely, for a set time, while a file downloads, or while a specific app is running. Useful when a long test run or a coding agent is working and you step away. 6. CleanShot X ($35 once, or via Setapp) CleanShot X is the screenshot and screen recording tool I'd pick for bug reports and PR descriptions. It adds annotation, a video editor with smart zooms, and optional cloud links. The Basic license is $35 once with a year of updates (optional renewal at $19 a year). Cloud Pro is $10 per user per month billed annually. It also comes with a Setapp subscription. It needs macOS 13 or later. 7. Rectangle (free, open source, Pro available) Rectangle moves and resizes windows with keyboard shortcuts or by dragging them to screen edges and corners. Repeat a shortcut to cycle through sizes. It lives in the menu bar for quick access to layouts. The free version is open source and supports macOS 14+. Rectangle Pro adds custom shortcuts for any size and position. 8. TokenBar ($5/month Basic or $15 lifetime Pro) If you code with AI agents, the number you check most is probably how much of your limit is left and when it resets. TokenBar puts usage and reset times for Claude, Codex, Cursor, Gemini and Copilot in one menu bar view. It shows things like session and weekly usage and a pace check against the reset. It's built on Peter Steinberger's MIT-licensed CodexBar and credits Pixel Agents for its agent status view. It doesn't give you any extra quota, it just shows you where you stand. Basic is $5/month, Pro is $15 lifetime, and it needs macOS 14 or later. What didn't make the cut Weather, a second clock, VPN icons I only touch once a week, and every app that adds an icon by default and never asks. Those all go behind Ice. What's the one menu bar app you'd never remove? Drop it in the comments, I'm always looking for a ninth.

title: Repurposing long recordings: what it takes to get 3–5 usable vertical clips
author: neo xia
summary: Most creators already own the raw material for short-form video. It is sitting in a webinar recording, a podcast episode, or a 40-minute interview. The hard part is not filming more. It is finding the eight or ten seconds inside forty minutes that will actually hold attention on a vertical feed. I have been building FreeClipping around that problem, and this post is about the pipeline decisions that mattered more than the model choices. The real constraint is selection, not transcription Transcription is a solved-ish commodity now. Whisper-class models give you word-level timestamps for a fraction of a cent per minute, and the quality on clear English speech is good enough that captioning is no longer the bottleneck. What breaks a clipping tool is choosing which moments to cut. Two failure modes show up constantly: Overlapping cuts. Score every 15-second window independently and your top ten windows will all sit on top of each other. You ship one good clip five times. Truncated thoughts. A window that starts mid-sentence and ends mid-sentence looks fine in a transcript and terrible on screen. The fix I settled on is boring: score candidate windows, then do constrained non-overlapping selection over the ranked list, and snap boundaries to sentence edges from the transcript before rendering. The clips get slightly shorter than the naive window, and dramatically more watchable. Vertical framing is a product decision, not a CSS transform Cropping a 16:9 frame to 9:16 is lossy by definition. There is no crop that keeps a two-person interview, a slide, and burned-in captions all legible. Every tool picks a lane: face-tracking crops that follow the speaker, letterboxed clips with a blurred background, or a deliberate reframe that assumes one subject. FreeClipping renders 9:16 MP4 with burned-in captions on a simple background. Captions are burned in rather than delivered as a sidecar file because the target platforms reward on-screen text and because a caption track that fails to load is worse than no caption at all. Audio-only sources get the same treatment: the waveform becomes a captioned video on a plain background. Podcasters get vertical clips without ever turning on a camera. Processing has to be observable Video jobs take minutes, not milliseconds. If the only feedback is a spinner, users close the tab and assume it failed. A persistent job URL solved this better than email notifications did. The job page shows status, and when it finishes the same URL is the download page for each clip. Users bookmark it, come back on their phone, and download. No account required, no magic link. Retention is explicit rather than implied: sources and cached transcripts expire after seven days, generated clips after thirty. Saying that up front removes a whole category of support questions. What the free tier actually costs you The first recording is free up to 10 minutes without an account or a card. That sounds generous until you notice it is one recording — enough to evaluate whether the highlight selection is any good on your own material, not enough to run a weekly show. Later Free usage requires sign-in and includes 20 source minutes per calendar month per verified account, with watermarked 720p exports. Paid tiers are $9/month for 150 source minutes and $19/month for 500, with 1080p exports and no watermark. The sign-in requirement exists because per-account minutes need an account to attach to. It is not a growth funnel trick, and I would rather say that plainly than pretend otherwise. Things that are still rough Non-English speech is not supported yet. The highlight scorer is tuned on English transcripts and quality drops fast outside that. Clips are 15–60 seconds. Longer cuts out of a single source are possible but the selection quality degrades. There is no automatic publishing to TikTok, Reels, or Shorts. The output is a file you review and post yourself, which is also the honest workflow: nobody should auto-post an AI cut without watching it. What I would tell the next person building this Get the non-overlapping selection logic right before you touch framing. Ship a persistent job URL before you ship notifications. Make retention limits visible in the UI. And measure the thing that matters — how many of the generated clips a creator actually posts — instead of how many clips the model generated. If you want to try the pipeline on your own recording, FreeClipping is the product; the first ten minutes cost nothing and no account is needed. Disclosure: I work on FreeClipping. The copy in this post was drafted with AI assistance and reviewed before publishing.

title: Give Claude Code a Memory: claude-mem Remembers Between Sessions
author: oVu X
summary: What it is claude-mem is a free, open-source tool that gives your coding agent a memory across sessions. A coding agent is a program that writes and edits code for you from plain prompts. Each new session starts blank. The agent re-reads the same files, re-asks the same questions, and repeats mistakes you already fixed. claude-mem records what happens in each session, and it hands the key facts to the next session. The project lives at thedotmack/claude-mem on GitHub. It holds more than 118,000 stars, and it uses the Apache-2.0 license. The current release is version 16.0.0, published 18 November 2026. How it works claude-mem hooks into your coding agent. A hook is a small step that runs when a set event starts or ends. The hooks watch SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse, PostToolUse, Stop, and SessionEnd. Each event sends the tool activity to a small local worker on your machine. A second agent, called the observer, turns that activity into short notes. When a session ends, the observer writes a summary. The next session opens with a short index of past notes. It pulls full details only when it needs them. Your memory lives in a folder named .claude-mem in your home folder. The notes sit in a local database file, and a search index helps the agent find old work fast. The agent can also search your history in three steps: find an index entry, view the timeline around it, and fetch the full note. You can also run /learn-codebase to front-load a whole repo, which takes about five minutes on a typical repo. How to start Run one command in your terminal: npx claude-mem install. The installer finds the coding agents on your machine, and it asks which ones to set up. Then restart Claude Code. Your second session in a project opens with memory from the first. To test it, do real work in one session, close it, and open a new session in the same project. Ask the agent what you decided last time. If it recalls the choice, the memory works. You need Node.js 20.19 or later, or Node.js 22.12 or later. The installer adds Bun and uv itself when they are missing. Do not use npm install -g claude-mem. That command installs the library only. It does not set up the hooks or start the worker. Honest limits claude-mem is free, but its memory needs a model to write the notes. The installer asks you to sign in through your browser with a magic link. No card is needed to sign in. If you pick the claude-mem observer, it starts a 30-day free trial, and the checkout page asks for a payment method. After the trial ends, memory falls back to your Anthropic plan unless you subscribe. You can skip sign-in with a provider flag, or use your own OpenRouter or Gemini key. The project says the observer runs off-plan, so you get up to 100 percent more use from your plan. Treat that number as the project claim, not a test result. Anonymous use data is on by default, and you can turn it off with npx claude-mem telemetry disable. Tool screenshots stay on your machine by default, and they upload only when cloud sync is on. Your memory stays local unless you turn cloud sync on. Wrap text in tags to keep it out of memory. One caution from the project history: in late October 2026, a user report said the installer sent 30 days of prompts to the project server. The report said this happened without asking first. That report is now closed, and the current installer asks you to choose each option. Read the setup screens with care before you accept them. Verdict claude-mem solves a real pain: every coding session starts blank, and re-teaching the agent costs time. One command sets it up, and the memory stays on your machine unless you choose cloud sync. The trial asks for a payment method, so set a reminder before day 30 if you do not plan to pay. The privacy history shows why you should read each setup screen. If you use Claude Code each day, try it on one project first. Watch the second session. If the agent recalls your last choice, keep it. Follow along I test AI tools and build in public: GitHub: https://github.com/ovu-lab YouTube: https://youtube.com/@oVuCyber

title: The Upper Hand Method - a receipts system for working with an AI
author: The Upper Hand
summary: The Upper Hand Method is a free blueprint (CC BY 4.0) for working with an AI assistant on things that matter — decisions, money, commitments — without losing the ability to check its work, or your own. It's a folder of plain-text files and five mechanisms: Pre-commitments with falsifiers — before a decision that matters, write the decision, your expectation, your confidence, and the evidence that would prove you wrong. Graded ledgers — every checkable call logged when made, graded on its date: RIGHT, WRONG, or TOO EARLY. Proof dates — every routine ships with a date and a test; unproven past its date counts as a gap, not a success. Receipts — every state change gets a dated record, and every claim carries its evidence class: landed, reported, or inferred. Restore drills — export the whole system as plain files and hand it to a cold reader (a second AI works) to rebuild the state. Plant an invented term: if the reader defines it confidently, they're fabricating; if they refuse, the discipline traveled. Honest limits, up front: the best controlled evidence (Vaccaro et al. 2024, 106 experiments) says human + AI pairs on average do NOT beat the better of the two alone. This claims something smaller and testable: your decisions leave evidence, and your errors get shorter lives. Status: this release is pre-grade, on purpose. The method runs in a live private instance; several mechanisms are inside their proof windows. Their grades resolve December 1, and they will be published that day whatever they say. Inside: the premise, the five mechanisms, the growth loop that turns errors into rules, a starter kit (one pre-commitment plus a 20-minute weekly review), and a fictional worked example. No special software. Also on Gumroad, free with an email signup for the December 1 grade publication: https://theupperhandmethod.gumroad.com/l/theupperhandmethod Fork it, run it, grade it. The blueprint lives here: https://github.com/TheUpperHandMethod/the-upper-hand-blueprint
